title: Replying to @🌈Elle💛 #theatre #shakespeare
transcript: What are some examples of Landlord Special Shakespeare? This is a question I got on a video where I use that term to describe Shakespeare in the Park's production of Romeo and Juliet. And as I said in that video, this is a term I used to describe any production, but especially with Shakespeare, where they use a concept that's kind of indiscriminately slathered over the play without really doing the work to implement it in a more granular, fine tuned way. And I do think there have been a lot of landlord special productions at Shakespeare in the park in the past. Maybe most notably where they did a Julius Caesar where Caesar was made to look like our current president. I did a whole video about the public reaction to this. It's very complicated and nuanced. But in either case, I don't think that they incorporated it into Julius Caesar very holistically. Also at Shakespeare in the park was Kenny Leon's version of much ado about nothing, where it very explicitly took place in Georgia before the Stacy Abrams election. Maybe something went over my head here, but I didn't think this had much to do with Much Ado at all. Or if it did, it wasn't implemented very clearly, or to its fullest potential. One of the more recent examples of this I saw was a production of Coriolanus at Theatre for a New Audience, which incorporated a kind of like surveillance video screen violence thing? Not only do I not think they implemented it very well, it was also kind of working against the play,in my opinion. I also think about this RSC Production of the Tempest from 2016. Essentially, they had, like, motion capture technology for the character of Ariel, and it was an interesting idea, but it didn't do much for the production. And it was also one of the most visually hideous things I've ever seen on stage. A couple of the Classical Theatre of Harlem productions have also been a little bit landlord special-y. This production of A Midsummer Night's Dream with a roaring 20s theme. And, you know, there's something in there with Midsummer, but I don't think it was done in a way that, like, really had that much effect on how the production played. They also had this production of Twelfth Night with an Afrofuturist theme. And this is where I wanna clarify something important, because I actually really loved this production. It was a really well done rendition of Twelfth Night and the Afrofuturist aesthetic was fun. It did kind of feel like it was just slapped on, at least as far as I could tell. Maybe something went over my head again, but in either case, it didn't ruin the production. Like, it's possible to do Landlord Special and the production is still just good. But let's talk about some productions that were *not* Landlord Special. I wouldn't say Robert Icke’s Hamlet had much of a clear concept, but it did have a very clear vision that was baked into every little tiny detail of the production. One hamlet that *did* have a very clear concept was Waterwell’s production starring Arian Moayed. This one was set in Persia right before World War 1 and sections of it were translated into Farsi. And it was done so thoughtfully and carefully that I actually thought to myself like, maybe Hamlet is a play about the Cultural Revolution in 20th century Persia. We also had the Donmar Shakespeare trilogy, which was three Shakespeare plays and the concept was that they were being performed by a group of inmates in a female prison. They managed to like tell a story outside of the play in the framing device where some of these inmates had their own character arc separate from what Shakespeare wrote. Another one that I think made great use of its concept was Merry Wives at Shakespeare in the park. This one was set in modern day Harlem and while I don't necessarily think that had a strong impact on the themes of the play, it was done in a way that felt very grounded where you could really feel that like this from the play would be the equivalent of this in modern day Harlem. And this was directed by Sahim Ali, who also did this year's Romeo and Juliet and last Year's Twelfth Night. So I don't know. Both of which I liked a lot less than this Merry Wives.
